title.en: The Council in Darkness: Earth Spoken into Being
title.zh: 黑暗中的議會：大地由言語而成

region.zh: 危地馬拉高地庫馬爾卡赫（烏塔特蘭）（象徵性定位）

texts.period: K'iche' text written c. 1554-78; Ximenez transcription c. 1701-03

source.work: Popol Wuj (K'iche' text c. 1554-78; transcription by Francisco Ximenez c. 1701-03), French ed. Brasseur de Bourbourg, 1861

texts.license: Public domain (Brasseur 1861 French edition); modern translations only paraphrased

summary.en: Before the world there is only sea, sky, and the gods gathered in darkness. The Framer, the Shaper, Sovereign Plumed Serpent, and Heart of Sky confer, and by merely speaking and thinking — agreeing on the ripening of the dawn — they raise the earth out of the water: mountains rise, valleys open, and the forests bring forth life.
summary.zh: 世界之前只有海洋、天空與在黑暗中聚合的諸神。塑造者、羽蛇主宰與天之心相商，僅憑言語與思想——就黎明的成熟達成一致——便將大地自水中升起：山巒隆起，谷地張開，森林萌發生命。

sensitivity.note: Living K'iche' tradition; the Popol Wuj is treated by some Maya communities as sacred counsel. Only published translations are paraphrased; no restricted or unpublished ceremonial text is reproduced.

passages.text: There is not yet one person, one animal, bird, fish, crab, tree, rock, hollow, canyon, meadow, or forest. Alone, the sky exists. The face of the earth has not appeared. There is only the sea's calm expanse and the expanse of heaven. Nothing has been brought together, nothing has been raised. The beach, the sea and the sky are the only things there are; nothing has gathered, only stillness, only silence, only night, only the lonely expanse.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 1 opening (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then the Framer and the Shaper, the Sovereign and Quetzal Serpent, the Bearer and Begetter, and Heart of Sky — Hurricane, Newborn Thunderbolt, Sudden Thunderbolt — come together and speak the ripening of the dawn in the darkness, in the night. They confer, ponder, and reflect, and what they agree upon is spoken: the earth rises like a cloud from the middle of the sea. Mountains appear from the water at once, and the valleys and ravines push apart; the cypresses and pines shoot forth on the ridges, and the meadows, vines, and bushes bloom.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 1 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Sovereign Plumed Serpent and Heart of Sky ask what has happened, and it is told: the earth has been raised, as it should be. The gods call it 'earth' in the gathering of light and shadow, of night and dawn. And the Framer and Shaper say: it was merely their word alone that brought it forth — no stone had been laid, no tree planted; by their thought alone the earth stood fast. This is the first sign of the place of the horizon where the dawn will come.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 1 (Brasseur 1861; Christenson 2003); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: Brasseur de Bourbourg, Popol Vuh (French, 1861); Dennis Tedlock, Popol Vuh, rev. ed. 1996

narrative.en:
The Popol Wuj opens with a cosmogony of pure speech. Before anything exists there is only stillness: the calm sea and the empty sky, night alone, and the gods assembled within it — the Framer and the Shaper, the Bearer and the Begetter, Hunahpu Pos, Hunahpu Utiu, the Sovereign and Quetzal Serpent (the great plumed serpent couple), the Heart of Lake, the Heart of Sea, and above all Heart of Sky, whose three aspects are Hurricane, Newborn Thunderbolt, and Sudden Thunderbolt, the trinity of storm gods who speak as one voice.

The gods talk together, think, and meditate upon the appearance of light, upon the dawn, upon what will need to exist for the people to be nourished. There is nothing yet: no person, no beast, no bird, no fish, no tree, no stone, no canyon, no meadow. Then comes the essential gesture of Maya creation: they agree on it in their minds, and they speak it. Merely by word and thought the earth is born. It rises like a cloud or like a mist from the sea; mountains come forth out of the water immediately and stand apart; the cypresses, pines, and gullies of the ridges shoot forth; the meadows and the vines and the bushes grow green. The Framer and the Shaper call it 'earth' in the presence of the sky, in the gathering of night and dawn.

Then Heart of Sky and Sovereign Plumed Serpent converse about the newly made earth. 'It has been raised,' they say; 'the earth is there, as it truly is.' They add the horizon: they make the small cords of light and shadow and the measures of night and dawn, and they mark the place of the horizon where the dawn will appear. Creation here is not a battle between cosmic opponents (as in Babylon or Norse myth) but a council: power flows from consensus, from a speech act ratified by every divine will present. This reflects the Maya political world, where authority required the agreement of councils and where words — oaths, day-names, prayers — carried causal weight.

The episode grounds everything that follows: the creations of animals, of mud and wood and maize people, are successive attempts to finish what this council began. Its ritual function is to authorize speech itself: what is said in agreement among the governing lines will stand, as the earth stood when the gods said 'earth'.

functions: Explains the origin of the earth as a speech act of divine council, authorizing councils and speech in K'iche' political life
Establishes Heart of Sky (Hurricane trio) as the storm triad that later floods the failed creations
Sets the horizon and the count of night and dawn, founding calendrical time

variants.name: Cakchiquel opening of the Annals
variants.summary: The Cakchiquel account likewise begins in darkness and the word: 'there was nothing yet, only the sea and the sky', and the creation proceeds from speech among the gods at Tulan before the crossing of the waters.

variants.name: Yucatec Chilam Balam creation
variants.text_tradition: Book of Chilam Balam of Chumayel (Roys trans. 1933)
variants.summary: The Yucatec 'creation of the world' likewise narrates a raising of the earth and the planting of the great world tree at the center, spoken into being and measured by the Bacabs.

texts.sensitivity_guidance: The Popol Wuj is a published, widely circulated text, but it remains sacred counsel for some K'iche' communities. Use published scholarly translations; paraphrase rather than reproduce copyrighted modern translations; do not present the text as 'dead lore'.

region.zh: 危地馬拉高地庫馬爾卡赫（烏塔特蘭）（象徵性定位）

texts.period: K'iche' text written c. 1554-78; Ximenez transcription c. 1701-03

source.work: Popol Wuj, Part 1, French ed. Brasseur de Bourbourg, 1861

texts.license: Public domain (Brasseur 1861 French edition); modern translations only paraphrased

summary.en: After the earth is raised, the grandmother Xmucane and the grandfather Xpiyacoc — the divine matchmakers and daykeepers — cast the corn kernels and the days to learn whether the world should be made. Their divination is itself a thing of the primordial night: asking the days before asking the gods.
summary.zh: 大地升起後，祖母徐穆坎與祖父希皮亞科克——神聖的媒合者與日守者——擲玉米粒與日名，以知世界是否應造。此占問本身即是太初黑夜中的事物：先問日子，再問神明。

sensitivity.note: Living K'iche' divinatory tradition; paraphrase of published translation only.

passages.text: Then Xmucane and Xpiyacoc, named as matchmakers, are called: grandmother of day, grandmother of light. The two of them speak in council about what should be done, and they divine: they sort the days and the corn kernels, casting them to see whether the making of the earth and the sky is a thing to be done or not done. This was the first divination, made while the world was still young, when the days themselves were newborn.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 1 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.

passages.text: The two daykeepers throw the kernels in fours, on the right and the left, reading the day signs that answer. It is the day itself that speaks to them in the throw, and they listen: the sign falls in the direction that shows the earth should be formed, and the forming of it is good. So the answer comes not as thunder but as a pattern of grains and day names — the same count that every later daykeeper of the K'iche' would consult before naming a child or planting a field.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 1 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.

title.en: The Animals Are Made and Condemned

region.zh: 危地馬拉高地庫馬爾卡赫（烏塔特蘭）（象徵性定位）

texts.period: K'iche' text written c. 1554-78; Ximenez transcription c. 1701-03

source.work: Popol Wuj, Part 1, French ed. Brasseur de Bourbourg, 1861

texts.license: Public domain (Brasseur 1861 French edition); modern translations only paraphrased

summary.en: Heart of Sky and the Plumed Serpent fashion the deer, birds, jaguars, and serpents and assign each its home and its food. But the animals can only squawk and howl — they cannot speak the names of their makers — so their flesh is sentenced to be caught and killed. Their speechlessness founds the human privilege of language and the eating of meat.
summary.zh: 天之心與羽蛇塑造鹿、鳥、美洲豹與蛇，並為其各定居所與食物。然而獸類只能鳴叫嘶吼——無法呼其造物者之名——故其肉身被判為可捕可食。獸之無言，奠基了人的語言特權與食肉之權。

sensitivity.note: Paraphrase of published translation; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Heart of Sky speaks to the Sovereign Plumed Serpent: the dawn has come, but the earth is empty of persons, of creatures that would tend it. So they make the animals of the mountains: the deer and the birds alone first, and they say to the deer, 'you shall walk in fours' — thus their legs — and to the birds, 'you shall live in the branches of the trees and in the vines.' Then the greater animals: jaguars, coyotes, peccaries, and serpents, each given its own den and its own way of feeding.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 1 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.

passages.text: But when the gods ask the animals to speak, to name their makers and pray to them, the animals can only squawk, chatter, and howl. They manage no words, each merely its own call. So the gods speak their sentence: 'You will be changed, because you could not make yourselves understood. Your flesh will be ground and eaten.' Thus it was settled that deer and birds would be caught and killed, and that their meat would feed those who could speak.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 1 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.

passages.text: The animals look for the rising of the sun, and they do not find it; they do not know where it will come from. This is why they are silent in the count of days: they have names for places but no words of praise. Having failed in speech, they are failed in turn, and they go to their mountains and their canyons, the homes assigned to them at the beginning.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 1 (Brasseur 1861; Christenson 2003); not verbatim.

title.en: The Mud People That Would Not Hold

region.zh: 危地馬拉高地庫馬爾卡赫（烏塔特蘭）（象徵性定位）

texts.period: K'iche' text written c. 1554-78; Ximenez transcription c. 1701-03

source.work: Popol Wuj, Part 1, French ed. Brasseur de Bourbourg, 1861

texts.license: Public domain (Brasseur 1861 French edition); modern translations only paraphrased

summary.en: The gods' first human figures are shaped of wet earth, but they crumble and dissolve: they cannot turn their heads, walk, or hold a shape. They are undone by water and left unfinished, the first failed attempt at humankind before wood and then maize.
summary.zh: 諸神最初以濕土塑人形，但泥人崩解消融：不能轉頭、行走，也無法保持形狀。他們被水所毀，成為造人未竟的第一次失敗——其後才有木人與玉米人。

sensitivity.note: Paraphrase of published translation; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: The gods speak again: 'Let us make one who will nourish and sustain us.' Then they try a figure of earth, mud, wet clay. It is molded and given a face, but it cannot move of itself; it cannot turn its head; it slides apart and collapses as if in water. Its strength dissolves, its face slumps; it cannot walk, and it cannot multiply.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 1 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Framer and the Shaper look at the mud people and speak among themselves: this is not what should be. The thing is lopsided and soft, without strength either to stand or to speak. So they take it apart and wash the earth away, and the first attempt is undone — the mud people are spoken of no more, except as the memory of a failure in the materials of the world.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 1 (Brasseur 1861; Christenson 2003); not verbatim.

title.en: The Hearthstones Bite: Tools Revolt Against the Wood People
title.zh: 灶石反噬：器物起而攻木人

region.zh: 危地馬拉高地庫馬爾卡赫（烏塔特蘭）（象徵性定位）

texts.period: K'iche' text written c. 1554-78; Ximenez transcription c. 1701-03

source.work: Popol Wuj, Part 1, French ed. Brasseur de Bourbourg, 1861

texts.license: Public domain (Brasseur 1861 French edition); modern translations only paraphrased

summary.en: When Heart of Sky destroys the wooden people with resinous rain, their own household implements rise against them: the grinding stones, cooking pots, dogs, and hearthstones that had been abused now gnash and bite, speaking the vengeance of tools. The survivors climb into the trees and become monkeys.
summary.zh: 天之心以松脂之雨毀滅木人時，其家中器物紛紛起而攻之：被虐待的石磨、陶鍋、狗與灶石出聲反擊，道出器物的復仇。倖存者攀樹而逃，化為猴子。

sensitivity.note: Paraphrase of published translation; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Then Heart of Sky blows a wind of resin through the sky, and a black rain falls day and night. The wooden people run everywhere, seeking shelter, but the shelters do not want them. The grinding stones say: 'You have beaten us and ground us without mercy; now it is our turn.' The cooking pots and cups answer: 'You have burned us over the fire and scraped us; now you will feel our teeth.' The dogs and the turkeys cry out and bite the faces of their masters.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 1 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.

passages.text: The hearthstones themselves — the three stones of the fireplace — rise up and throw themselves out of the fire at the wooden people, and the tortilla griddles spin at their heads. All of them flee to their houses, but the houses collapse, to the trees, but the trees shake them off, to the caves, but the caves shut before them. Only a few get away up high, and these become the monkeys in the trees, which is why the monkeys look like the shape of a person — a parody of humanity left over from the third creation.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 1 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.

region.zh: 危地馬拉高地庫馬爾卡赫（烏塔特蘭）（象徵性定位）

texts.period: K'iche' text written c. 1554-78; Ximenez transcription c. 1701-03

source.work: Popol Wuj, Part 1, French ed. Brasseur de Bourbourg, 1861

texts.license: Public domain (Brasseur 1861 French edition); modern translations only paraphrased

summary.en: Between the failed creations and the true dawn, Vucub Caquix, Seven Macaw, boasts in a nance tree: 'I am the sun, I am the moon, I am the light of the world.' His glittering metal teeth and eyes dazzle the survivors of the flood, and the world is lit only by his vanity until two boys come with a blowgun.
summary.zh: 在失敗的創造與真正的黎明之間，武庫布·卡魁希（七鸚鵡）於南美櫻桃樹上自誇：「我是太陽、月亮、世界之光。」其金屬牙齒與眼珠光耀炫目，炫惑洪水倖存者；直至兩個男孩持吹箭而來，世界只由其虛榮照明。

sensitivity.note: Paraphrase of published translation; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: This was when there was still no sun: Vucub Caquix would climb his nance tree and cry out: 'I am great! My place is higher than the human. I am their sun and their moon, and my light shines on the whole world. I am the guide for those who walk. My beak of metal shines; my teeth glitter with jewels. I am the eyes of the earth.' And the glitter of his mouth was so great that it cast a light over the earth, and everyone looked up at him in the dark before the true dawn.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 1 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.

passages.text: But he was not the sun, only a bird swollen with pride, his mouth and eyes of chipped metal that the gods destined for the grave. Heart of Sky speaks of him with anger: this one is not right; he would be a sun and a moon by vanity alone. And the two boys, Hunahpu and Xbalanque, are told to bring him down, for the true dawn must not be preceded by a counterfeit.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 1 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.

title.en: The Twins Shoot Seven Macaw and Take His Teeth
title.zh: 雙子射七鸚鵡而取其牙

region.zh: 危地馬拉高地庫馬爾卡赫（烏塔特蘭）（象徵性定位）

texts.period: K'iche' text written c. 1554-78; Ximenez transcription c. 1701-03

source.work: Popol Wuj, Part 1, French ed. Brasseur de Bourbourg, 1861

texts.license: Public domain (Brasseur 1861 French edition); modern translations only paraphrased

summary.en: Hunahpu and Xbalanque ambush Seven Macaw with a blowgun, breaking his jaw; posing as curers, they pull out his metal teeth and eyes, replacing them with grains of maize. The false sun, blinded, dies and is buried by his wife — the first of the monsters cleared away before the true sun can rise.
summary.zh: 烏納普與斯巴蘭克以吹箭伏擊七鸚鵡，擊碎其顎；繼而扮作醫者，拔除其金屬牙與眼，代以玉米粒。偽日盲目而亡，由其妻埋葬——真日升起前的第一個被清除的妖物。

sensitivity.note: Paraphrase of published translation; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: The two boys hide beneath the nance tree with their blowguns. Seven Macaw comes to eat the fruit, craning his neck, and Hunahpu shoots him in the jaw: the pellet breaks the metal mouth and the beak hangs crooked. Screaming, the great bird falls through the branches and seizes Hunahpu's arm in his beak, tearing it from its socket; then he flies up to his home on the hard rock, dragging the arm.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 1 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.

passages.text: The boys confer and send an old man and an old woman — the daykeepers in disguise — to serve as curers. They go up to Seven Macaw, who, crippled and dazzled, asks them to treat his mouth. They say his teeth must come out and be replaced, and he consents: they take out his glittering teeth one by one, putting in grains of white maize instead, and then remove the metal disks of his eyes.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 1 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.

passages.text: Once his teeth and eyes are gone, Seven Macaw is no longer brilliant; he dulls and dies, and his wife buries him on the rock. Hunahpu's arm is recovered and set right with a substitute of maize made by the daykeepers, and the false sun's rule of glitter is ended. It is the first great deed of the twins, done while the true sun is still sleeping under the earth.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 1 (Brasseur 1861; Christenson 2003); not verbatim.

title.en: Zipacna and the Four Hundred Boys

region.zh: 危地馬拉高地庫馬爾卡赫（烏塔特蘭）（象徵性定位）

texts.period: K'iche' text written c. 1554-78; Ximenez transcription c. 1701-03

source.work: Popol Wuj, Part 1, French ed. Brasseur de Bourbourg, 1861

texts.license: Public domain (Brasseur 1861 French edition); modern translations only paraphrased

summary.en: The Four Hundred Boys drag a great log to build their house and order the giant Zipacna into a pit to serve as a post — intending to bury him alive. He saves the wood by setting it on his shoulders and plays dead; that night they pour ash on the pit and celebrate his death. He bursts out and brings their house down on all four hundred, who become the Pleiades.
summary.zh: 四百男孩拖來大木建屋，命巨人希帕克納入坑充作柱——意圖將其活埋。他持木於肩、裝死脫身；當夜眾人傾灰於坑，慶其已死。巨人破土而出，令房屋塌落壓斃四百男孩，他們化為昴宿（四百星）。

sensitivity.note: Paraphrase of published translation; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: The Four Hundred Boys are dragging a large tree from the forest for the center pole of their house, and they cannot budge it. Zipacna comes to help them and carries the log alone. They flatter him into a dug pit to be a post in its place, and he suspects nothing; but they plan to drop the beam on him and bury him, for they have agreed among themselves that the strongman must die.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 1 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.

passages.text: He climbs out secretly, stands a severed arm in the pit to trick them, and waits while they pour ash and sand over the place and dance and drink, calling him dead. Then he rises like an ant out of the pit, and while they are all inside their new house — singing, drunk, celebrating their treachery — he lifts the great post and brings the whole roof down on them.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 1 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.

passages.text: All of the Four Hundred die there, and only one escapes, wounded; he goes to tell the daykeepers, who weep over the deaths. And the Four Hundred Boys went up into the sky to become the Pleiades, the little cluster called the Four Hundred, stars together on clear nights — a sign in the sky of the house that fell on its builders.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 1 (Brasseur 1861; Christenson 2003); not verbatim.

title.en: Zipacna and the Crab: The Mountain-Maker Drowns
title.zh: 希帕克納與蟹：造山者溺亡

region.zh: 危地馬拉高地庫馬爾卡赫（烏塔特蘭）（象徵性定位）

texts.period: K'iche' text written c. 1554-78; Ximenez transcription c. 1701-03

source.work: Popol Wuj, Part 1, French ed. Brasseur de Bourbourg, 1861

texts.license: Public domain (Brasseur 1861 French edition); modern translations only paraphrased

summary.en: Zipacna boasts of rolling up mountains by hand and of hunting only crabs, refusing birds and deer. The twins forge a lure — a bird carved and painted, filled with poison — and the grandmother declares the bird is crab meat. Zipacna chases the carved crab into a canyon, is buried to the waist, and drowns in a rock fissure turned to stone.
summary.zh: 希帕克納自誇徒手造山，且只獵蟹，不屑禽鳥走獸。雙子製作誘餌——雕繪並內藏毒物的假鳥——祖母則訛稱那是蟹肉。希帕克納追逐假蟹至峽谷，半身沒入土中，終溺斃於化為磐石的岩隙。

sensitivity.note: Paraphrase of published translation; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Zipacna declares what he eats: 'I hunt crabs, only crabs. I do not want birds or deer; I want the food of the water.' And each day he rolls up great mountains, making them by lifting and setting them, naming them as he goes — the claim of a maker of the world. But the twins have decided that the maker of mountains must be taken away, and they confer with their grandmother, the daykeeper.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 1 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.

passages.text: They carve a bird of wood, paint it, and fill it with poison, and show it to him as it soars. Zipacna reaches for it and it rises; the grandmother, as arranged, tells him it is not a bird at all but crab meat on the wing. So the giant goes after it as after a crab, and the painted decoy leads him to a canyon, where it folds into the earth like a crab into its hole.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 1 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.

passages.text: He digs after it and the canyon closes on him to his waist; he struggles and goes deeper, only his head above ground. Then he is covered by a mountain of rock and earth, and the place is called Split Earth. So dies the maker of mountains, drowned in the earth he loved to raise — and the twins go on to the next monster.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 1 (Brasseur 1861; Christenson 2003); not verbatim.

title.en: Cabracan the Mountain-Shaker Is Brought Down

region.zh: 危地馬拉高地庫馬爾卡赫（烏塔特蘭）（象徵性定位）

texts.period: K'iche' text written c. 1554-78; Ximenez transcription c. 1701-03

source.work: Popol Wuj, Part 1, French ed. Brasseur de Bourbourg, 1861

texts.license: Public domain (Brasseur 1861 French edition); modern translations only paraphrased

summary.en: Cabracan, second son of Seven Macaw, topples mountains for pleasure and claims to shake the earth. The twins offer him a roasted bird that is poisoned; when he eats it and sets out to destroy the ridges again, the mountains collapse under him and he dies beneath them, with his eyes bound.
summary.zh: 七鸚鵡次子卡布拉坎以掀翻群山為樂，自詡能撼動大地。雙子獻上烤鳥，內藏毒物；他食之，再欲毀山脊時，群山傾頹將其壓斃，其目被縛，死於所愛撼動之山之下。

sensitivity.note: Paraphrase of published translation; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: Cabracan is even prouder than his brother the mountain-maker: he shakes the earth and levels its ridges, and where he passes the mountains fall flat. The gods who made the ridges hear the quake and speak: 'It is not yet time for this; it will be in truth before the sun comes out. This one must be taken.' And the two boys go to meet him on his road.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 1 (Brasseur 1861; Tedlock 1996); not verbatim.

passages.text: The twins offer him a roasted bird, saying it is the meat he hunts. He eats it, and it is filled with poison. Then he goes to shake the mountains and cannot lift his arms; the ridges collapse around him, pinning him fast, and his eyes are bound. In the falls of the earth the mountain-shaker dies with his face to the ground, and the last of the three great monsters is cleared from the world before the dawn.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Popol Wuj, Part 1 (Brasseur 1861; Christenson 2003); not verbatim.
